Week 16 · Phase 4: Advanced Topics

Efficient and Scalable Deep Learning

Making deep learning fit, run fast and ship. GPU memory hierarchy, arithmetic intensity and the roofline model, profiling and bottleneck analysis, mixed precision (FP16 vs BF16, loss scaling), gradient accumulation and checkpointing (the sqrt(n) trade-off derived), data/tensor/pipeline parallelism, ZeRO and FSDP memory accounting, FlashAttention (online softmax derived), KV caching and speculative decoding, pruning, quantization (PTQ, QAT, int8/int4, GPTQ/AWQ), distillation, low-rank factorization, Mixture-of-Experts, NAS, and deployment with ONNX, TorchScript, torch.compile and serving. The lab profiles a training loop and applies AMP, quantization and distillation while reporting accuracy and latency trade-offs.

104 min read4 interactive demos17 figures24 code blocks10 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Describe the GPU memory hierarchy and explain why most deep-learning operations are limited by memory traffic rather than arithmetic.
  • Compute the arithmetic intensity of an operation, place it on a roofline, and decide whether it is memory-bound or compute-bound.
  • Profile a PyTorch training loop with torch.profiler, read the result, and separate data-loading, launch-overhead, memory-bound and compute-bound bottlenecks.
  • Explain FP16, BF16 and TF32, why FP16 needs loss scaling and BF16 usually does not, and train with torch.autocast.
  • Use gradient accumulation to emulate large batches, and gradient checkpointing to trade compute for memory, deriving the n\sqrt nn​ optimum.
  • Account for training memory (parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations) and predict what ZeRO stages 1 to 3 and FSDP save.
  • Explain data, tensor, pipeline and hybrid parallelism, ring all-reduce cost, and the pipeline bubble fraction.
  • Derive online softmax and the tiled FlashAttention algorithm, and explain why it is faster although it does not reduce FLOPs.
  • Explain KV caching, its memory cost, and the idea behind speculative decoding.
  • Apply and analyze pruning, post-training and quantization-aware quantization, distillation with the Hinton loss, and low-rank factorization.
  • Describe sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing and the load-balancing loss, and give an overview of neural architecture search.
  • Export and accelerate a model with torch.compile, TorchScript and ONNX, and reason about serving and edge constraints.

For the past fifteen weeks the question was "what model and what loss". This week the question is "what does it cost, and how do I make it cheaper without making it worse". The question has become unavoidable. A 7-billion-parameter language model needs over 100 GB just to train with Adam, which is more than any single GPU holds. Serving the same model to many users is limited less by arithmetic than by how fast bytes can be moved out of memory. A model that scores well in a notebook but needs a data-center GPU is useless on a phone. Efficiency is also the precondition for research: the experiments in your project run only as fast as your training loop does, and a loop that wastes 70% of the GPU makes you three times slower than you need to be.

The unifying idea is that computation is cheap and data movement is expensive. A modern GPU can perform hundreds of floating-point operations in the time it takes to fetch one number from main memory. Almost every technique this week is a way of reducing data movement, reducing the number of bytes per number, or splitting the data over more devices: mixed precision and quantization shrink the bytes; FlashAttention and operator fusion avoid round trips to memory; checkpointing and ZeRO trade extra computation or communication for less storage; pruning, distillation and low-rank factorization shrink the model itself; parallelism spreads what remains over many chips. Keep the question "where are the bytes, and how many times do they move?" in mind throughout.

The week is organized as a ladder. We start with the hardware and a simple model of performance (the roofline), then learn to measure (profiling). Next come the training-side tools that fit bigger models and batches onto a device (mixed precision, accumulation, checkpointing), then distributed training for when one device is not enough. FlashAttention and KV caching apply the same logic to the transformer's most expensive operator. We then turn to making finished models smaller and faster (compression, Mixture-of-Experts, architecture search), and finish with deployment and a lab that measures the trade-offs.

Hardware: how a GPU actually works

Throughput processors and the memory hierarchy

A CPU is built to run one thread of irregular code quickly: big caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution. A GPU is built to run thousands of nearly identical threads at once and to hide the latency of memory behind sheer parallelism. An NVIDIA A100, a typical 2020-era training GPU, has 108 streaming multiprocessors (SMs). Each SM contains 64 FP32 cores, four tensor cores (units that multiply small matrix tiles, for example 16×8×1616\times 8\times 1616×8×16, in a single instruction) and a register file. Threads are grouped into warps of 32 that execute the same instruction in lockstep, and warps are grouped into thread blocks that are scheduled onto SMs. The tensor cores are where deep learning lives: on the A100 they deliver 312 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 or FP16 arithmetic, against about 19.5 TFLOP/s for ordinary FP32 cores. That 16-fold gap is a major reason mixed precision matters.

Arithmetic is only half the story. Data must reach the cores, and the memory system is a hierarchy:

  • Registers are private to each thread and effectively free to access, but scarce (256 KB per SM).
  • Shared memory / L1 is a programmer-managed scratchpad on each SM, up to 164 KB, with bandwidth an order of magnitude above HBM. Fast kernels load a tile of data here once and reuse it many times. We call this level SRAM below.
  • L2 cache (40 MB on A100) is shared across SMs.
  • HBM (high-bandwidth memory), also called global or device memory, is the 40 or 80 GB where your tensors live. Its bandwidth is 1.5 to 2.0 TB/s on an A100 and 3.35 TB/s on an H100 SXM. This number sets the speed of every operation that touches each element once.
  • Host memory is reached over PCIe (about 32 GB/s per direction for PCIe 4.0 x16), roughly 60 times slower than HBM. Moving tensors between CPU and GPU in the inner loop is a classic performance bug. Between GPUs, NVLink provides about 600 GB/s per GPU on the A100 and 900 GB/s on the H100, and between servers a network (InfiniBand or Ethernet) provides 10 to 50 GB/s per GPU.

The cost of moving data dominates the cost of computing with it. A useful mental model: the A100's tensor cores can perform about 150 FLOPs in the time HBM delivers a single byte (312 TFLOP/s divided by 2 TB/s), which is about 300 FLOPs per 2-byte FP16 number. Any operation that does only a handful of FLOPs per number it reads is therefore starved for data.

TPUs and other accelerators

Google's TPU takes a different design point. Instead of many programmable SMs, a TPU core is built around a large systolic array (a 128×128128\times128128×128 grid of multiply-accumulate units in the early generations) fed from on-chip memory, with a compiler (XLA) that plans all data movement ahead of time. TPUs are connected in a fixed 2-D or 3-D torus network ("pods") that makes the collective operations used in large-scale training fast. The preferred number format is BF16, which Google introduced for this hardware. The trade-off against GPUs is flexibility: TPUs favour large, regular, statically shaped computations and reward you for expressing your program in JAX or through XLA. The concepts in this chapter (bandwidth versus compute, memory hierarchy, collective communication) apply to both. Other accelerators (AMD Instinct, Intel Gaudi, Apple's GPU and Neural Engine, mobile NPUs) share the same structure: a lot of matrix arithmetic fed by a comparatively narrow memory pipe.

Why BF16 exists

Mixed-precision training with FP16 was popularized by Micicevicius et al. (2018, NVIDIA and Baidu). Google Brain designed bfloat16 ("brain floating point") for TPUs: take the FP32 format, keep all 8 exponent bits and truncate the mantissa to 7 bits. Conversion from FP32 is just dropping the low 16 bits, and the dynamic range equals FP32's, which removes the need for loss scaling. NVIDIA added BF16 tensor cores in the A100 (2020), and it has since become the default training format for large models.

Arithmetic intensity and the roofline model

Two ways to be slow

Any kernel needs to do FFF floating-point operations and to move QQQ bytes between main memory and the chip. If the device can perform PPP FLOP/s and move BBB bytes/s, the kernel cannot finish faster than the larger of the two times:

t  ≥  max⁡ ⁣(FP,  QB).t \;\ge\; \max\!\left(\frac{F}{P},\; \frac{Q}{B}\right).t≥max(PF​,BQ​).

Dividing by FFF and defining the arithmetic intensity I=F/QI = F/QI=F/Q (FLOP per byte moved), the best achievable throughput is

attainable FLOP/s  =  min⁡(P,  B⋅I).\text{attainable FLOP/s} \;=\; \min\bigl(P,\; B\cdot I\bigr).attainable FLOP/s=min(P,B⋅I).

Plotted against III on log-log axes this is the roofline model (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009): a sloped line of slope BBB (the "memory roof") that meets a flat line at height PPP (the "compute roof") at the ridge point I∗=P/BI^* = P/BI∗=P/B. An operation left of the ridge is memory-bound: speeding up the arithmetic does nothing, only moving fewer bytes helps. An operation right of the ridge is compute-bound: only faster math (tensor cores, lower precision) helps.

For the A100 with BF16 tensor cores, P=312P = 312P=312 TFLOP/s and B≈2.0B \approx 2.0B≈2.0 TB/s, so I∗≈153I^* \approx 153I∗≈153 FLOP/byte. For the H100 SXM, P≈989P \approx 989P≈989 TFLOP/s (dense BF16) and B=3.35B = 3.35B=3.35 TB/s, so I∗≈295I^* \approx 295I∗≈295. The ridge has moved right with each generation, because compute grows faster than bandwidth: more and more operations fall on the memory-bound side.

Intensity of the operations you use

Arithmetic intensity of a matrix multiply

Multiply A∈RM×KA\in\R^{M\times K}A∈RM×K by B∈RK×NB\in\R^{K\times N}B∈RK×N into C∈RM×NC\in\R^{M\times N}C∈RM×N, with bbb bytes per element. The work is F=2MNKF = 2MNKF=2MNK (one multiply and one add per term). The minimum traffic reads AAA and BBB and writes CCC: Q=b(MK+KN+MN)Q = b(MK + KN + MN)Q=b(MK+KN+MN). So

I=2MNKb (MK+KN+MN).I = \frac{2MNK}{b\,(MK+KN+MN)}.I=b(MK+KN+MN)2MNK​.

Square case. With M=N=K=nM=N=K=nM=N=K=n: I=2n33bn2=2n3bI = \dfrac{2n^3}{3bn^2} = \dfrac{2n}{3b}I=3bn22n3​=3b2n​. In FP16 (b=2b=2b=2) this is n/3n/3n/3. To pass the A100 ridge of 153 you need n≳460n \gtrsim 460n≳460. A 256×256256\times256256×256 FP16 matmul has I≈85I\approx 85I≈85 and runs at only 2.0 TB/s×85=1742.0\text{ TB/s}\times 85 = 1742.0 TB/s×85=174 TFLOP/s at best, while a 1024×10241024\times10241024×1024 one is compute-bound.

Matrix-vector case (M=1M=1M=1, the situation when generating one token at a time). The term KNKNKN (the weight matrix) dominates the traffic: I≈2NKbNK=2bI\approx \dfrac{2NK}{bNK}=\dfrac 2bI≈bNK2NK​=b2​, which is 1 FLOP/byte in FP16, 150 times below the ridge. The GPU runs at under 1% of peak. The only way to speed up decoding is to move fewer bytes: quantize the weights, batch more requests together (raising MMM), or use a smaller model.

Elementwise operations are even worse. Adding two FP16 tensors performs 1 FLOP per element but moves 6 bytes (read two, write one): I≈0.17I\approx 0.17I≈0.17. The same holds for ReLU, dropout, residual additions, LayerNorm and softmax, which perform a few FLOPs per element. These memory-bound operations are individually trivial in FLOPs yet can account for a large share of the run time of a transformer, because each launches its own kernel and makes its own trip through HBM.

Fusion and the "memory wall"

If memory traffic is the problem, the cure is to do more per trip. Operator fusion combines consecutive memory-bound operations into one kernel: instead of writing the output of x + bias to HBM and reading it back for the ReLU, a fused kernel keeps the value in registers and writes only the final result. A chain of kkk elementwise operations done separately costs about kkk round trips; fused it costs one. Fusion is what compilers (torch.compile, XLA, TVM) do automatically, and it is the same principle that makes FlashAttention fast. Remember the pattern: matmuls are compute-bound if large enough; everything else is memory-bound, and the job is to avoid trips to HBM. This is also why the same mathematical operation can differ 10-fold in speed depending on implementation.

Counting FLOPs is not counting time

FLOP counts (for example "6ND FLOPs to train a transformer with NNN parameters on DDD tokens", Week 10) tell you the compute-bound time. The real time also includes memory-bound operators, kernel-launch overhead, communication and data loading. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU, the ratio of achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware peak) is the standard summary. Well-tuned large-scale LLM training reaches 40 to 60% MFU. A naive PyTorch loop on a small model often reaches under 10%.

Profiling and bottleneck analysis

"Premature optimization is the root of all evil" applies doubly to deep learning, where intuition about performance is usually wrong. Measure first. The workflow is: (1) get an end-to-end number (samples per second, step time, GPU utilization); (2) find where the time goes; (3) classify the bottleneck; (4) fix the biggest one; (5) re-measure.

Measuring correctly

GPU kernels run asynchronously: when Python calls y = model(x), PyTorch enqueues kernels and returns immediately. If you time with time.time() you measure how long it took to enqueue. You must call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock (or use CUDA events). You should also warm up (the first iterations include CUDA context creation, cuDNN autotuning and memory allocation), run many iterations, and report a median rather than a single value.

pythonbenchmark.py
import time
import torch

def bench(fn, warmup=10, iters=50):
    """Median wall-clock time of fn() in milliseconds, with correct GPU synchronization."""
    use_cuda = torch.cuda.is_available()
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn()
    if use_cuda:
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        if use_cuda:
            torch.cuda.synchronize()          # wait until all queued kernels finish
        times.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1e3)
    times.sort()
    return times[len(times) // 2]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    dev = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    for n in (256, 1024, 4096):
        a = torch.randn(n, n, device=dev, dtype=torch.float16 if dev == "cuda" else torch.float32)
        ms = bench(lambda: a @ a)
        tflops = 2 * n ** 3 / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e12
        print(f"n={n:5d}  {ms:8.3f} ms  {tflops:7.1f} TFLOP/s")

Run this on a GPU and you will see achieved TFLOP/s rise steeply with nnn and saturate, exactly the roofline's prediction. (On an A100 the 256256256 case typically reaches only a fraction of the compute roof because it is both memory-bound and too small to occupy 108 SMs.)

The PyTorch profiler

torch.profiler records every CPU-side operator and CUDA kernel with timestamps. The usual recipe wraps a few training steps with a schedule that skips start-up noise:

pythonprofile_loop.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.profiler import profile, record_function, schedule, ProfilerActivity, tensorboard_trace_handler

dev = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1024, 4096), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4096, 1024)).to(dev)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
x = torch.randn(256, 1024, device=dev)
y = torch.randn(256, 1024, device=dev)

activities = [ProfilerActivity.CPU] + ([ProfilerActivity.CUDA] if dev == "cuda" else [])
sched = schedule(wait=1, warmup=2, active=3, repeat=1)   # skip 1 step, warm up 2, record 3

with profile(activities=activities, schedule=sched, record_shapes=True,
             profile_memory=True, on_trace_ready=tensorboard_trace_handler("./prof")) as prof:
    for step in range(7):
        with record_function("forward"):
            loss = ((model(x) - y) ** 2).mean()
        with record_function("backward"):
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss.backward()
        with record_function("optimizer"):
            opt.step()
        prof.step()                                       # tell the profiler a step ended

sort_key = "cuda_time_total" if dev == "cuda" else "cpu_time_total"
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by=sort_key, row_limit=8))

Open the trace with TensorBoard (pip install torch_tb_profiler, tensorboard --logdir prof) or load the generated JSON in chrome://tracing / Perfetto. In the timeline, look at the GPU stream row. Gaps between kernels mean the GPU is idle waiting for the CPU. In the operator table, sort by total CUDA time and check the top five rows. (Recent PyTorch versions are renaming cuda_time_total to device_time_total; if the key is rejected, pick the nearest column name in the printed table header.)

Diagnosing the bottleneck

A GPU job is limited by one of five things. The symptoms are distinct:

Bottleneck Symptom in nvidia-smi / trace Typical fix
Input pipeline (data loading, augmentation, host-to-device copy) GPU utilization oscillates and falls to 0% between steps; the DataLoader wait appears at the start of each step more num_workers, pin_memory=True, persistent_workers=True, prefetch, cheaper augmentation, faster storage format, do augmentations on the GPU
CPU / launch overhead many tiny kernels of a few microseconds each, with gaps; common for small models, small batches and Python-heavy code larger batch, fuse with torch.compile, CUDA graphs, remove Python loops and .item() calls
Memory-bound kernels elementwise ops, normalizations, softmax, and attention dominating GPU time; low achieved FLOP/s fusion (torch.compile), FlashAttention, lower precision
Compute-bound large GEMMs/convolutions dominate and run near peak mixed precision/tensor cores, smaller model, better algorithm
Communication (multi-GPU) NCCL all-reduce kernels not overlapped with compute; ranks wait for each other overlap (DDP does this), larger buckets, gradient accumulation, faster interconnect, sharding strategy

Two cheap diagnostics are worth memorizing. First, run the model on a single cached batch in a loop: if throughput jumps, the data pipeline was the bottleneck. Second, double the batch size: if time per step barely changes, you were launch-bound (the GPU had spare capacity); if it doubles, you were compute- or bandwidth-bound.

Always check utilization before optimizing the model

The most common finding by far, in student projects, is not that the model is slow but that the GPU is idle because the loop does CPU-side work, synchronizes with loss.item() or print every step, or loads images with a single worker. Fix this first. Mixed precision on a loop that spends 60% of its time waiting for data gives you almost nothing.

Mixed-precision training

Number formats

Floating-point numbers store a sign, an exponent (which sets the range) and a mantissa (which sets the precision). The formats you will meet:

Format Bits Exponent Mantissa Max finite Smallest normal Unit roundoff uuu
FP32 32 8 23 3.4×10383.4\times10^{38}3.4×1038 1.2×10−381.2\times10^{-38}1.2×10−38 6×10−86\times10^{-8}6×10−8
TF32 (tensor-core math, stored as FP32) 19 used 8 10 3.4×10383.4\times10^{38}3.4×1038 1.2×10−381.2\times10^{-38}1.2×10−38 5×10−45\times10^{-4}5×10−4
FP16 16 5 10 65,504 6.1×10−56.1\times10^{-5}6.1×10−5 (subnormals down to 6×10−86\times10^{-8}6×10−8) 4.9×10−44.9\times10^{-4}4.9×10−4
BF16 16 8 7 3.4×10383.4\times10^{38}3.4×1038 1.2×10−381.2\times10^{-38}1.2×10−38 3.9×10−33.9\times10^{-3}3.9×10−3

Unit roundoff u=2−(p+1)u=2^{-(p+1)}u=2−(p+1) is the worst-case relative rounding error of one operation, where ppp is the number of mantissa bits. FP16 has three more bits of precision than BF16 (about three decimal digits versus two) but only a 5-bit exponent, so its dynamic range is narrow: values above 65,504 overflow to infinity and values below roughly 6×10−86\times10^{-8}6×10−8 flush to zero. BF16 trades precision for range: it can represent anything FP32 can, in coarser steps. TF32 is an A100 feature: matmuls take FP32 inputs, round them to 10 mantissa bits internally and accumulate in FP32; you enable it with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True (or torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")) and need no other code change. FP8 formats (E4M3 and E5M2) on H100-class hardware extend the same story one step further.

The recipe of Micicevicius et al.

Simply casting a network to FP16 fails for two reasons. The update problem: weights are updated by small increments Δw=η g\Delta w=\eta\,gΔw=ηg, and with a 10-bit mantissa an increment smaller than about w×2−11w\times 2^{-11}w×2−11 is rounded away entirely. A weight of 1.0 cannot change by less than 0.0005. The range problem: gradients are often tiny (activation gradients of 10−810^{-8}10−8 are common), below FP16's representable range, so they underflow to zero and learning silently stalls.

The recipe in Mixed Precision Training (Micicevicius et al., ICLR 2018) has three parts:

  1. FP32 master weights. Keep an FP32 copy of the parameters. The forward and backward passes use an FP16 copy (so activations and activation gradients are 16-bit and matmuls use tensor cores), but the optimizer updates the FP32 master copy and then re-casts it to FP16. Updates accumulate in a format that can represent them.
  2. Loss scaling. Multiply the loss by a large constant SSS (for example 2162^{16}216) before backward. By the chain rule every gradient is multiplied by SSS, which shifts the gradient distribution up into FP16's representable range. Before the optimizer step, divide the gradients by SSS (in FP32) to recover the true values.
  3. FP32 accumulation for sensitive operations. Matmul and convolution accumulate partial sums in FP32 even when the inputs are FP16; reductions such as softmax, layer norm statistics, losses and batch-norm variances are done in FP32.

Dynamic loss scaling automates the choice of SSS. Start high; if any gradient contains inf or NaN (overflow), skip that optimizer step and halve SSS; if many consecutive steps (say 2000) are clean, double SSS. This is the algorithm in torch.amp.GradScaler.

BF16 needs no loss scaling

With BF16's FP32-sized exponent, gradients that are representable in FP32 are essentially representable in BF16, so underflow is not an issue and the scaler is unnecessary. The price is precision: a 7-bit mantissa has u≈0.4%u\approx 0.4\%u≈0.4%, so you rely even more on FP32 master weights and FP32 accumulation to keep training stable. In practice BF16 mixed precision is simpler, more robust and the standard on hardware that supports it (Ampere and newer, TPUs); FP16 remains relevant on older GPUs (V100, T4) and for inference.

Mixed precision in PyTorch

torch.autocast is a context manager that chooses the precision per operator: matmuls, convolutions and linear layers run in 16-bit; operations that are numerically sensitive (softmax, log-softmax, losses, norms, reductions, exp, pow) run in FP32. Parameters stay in FP32 (they are the master weights), and autocast casts copies on the fly.

pythonamp_train.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

dev = "cuda"
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 2048), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(2048, 10)).to(dev)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# FP16 needs loss scaling; BF16 does not. Pick based on hardware support.
use_bf16 = torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()
amp_dtype = torch.bfloat16 if use_bf16 else torch.float16
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda", enabled=not use_bf16)   # a no-op when disabled

x = torch.randn(256, 784, device=dev)
y = torch.randint(0, 10, (256,), device=dev)

for step in range(100):
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=amp_dtype):
        logits = model(x)                       # linear layers run in 16-bit tensor-core matmuls
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y)       # cross_entropy is autocast to float32
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()               # backward of (loss * scale)
    scaler.unscale_(opt)                        # gradients back to true scale, in place
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)   # clip AFTER unscale
    scaler.step(opt)                            # skips the step if any grad is inf/NaN
    scaler.update()                             # adjusts the scale factor
    if step % 20 == 0:
        print(step, f"loss={loss.item():.4f}", f"scale={scaler.get_scale():.0f}",
              "logits dtype:", logits.dtype, "param dtype:", next(model.parameters()).dtype)

Note the outputs of the last line: logits are 16-bit (the linear layer's output dtype) while the parameters remain torch.float32. Two details commonly go wrong. Gradient clipping must happen after scaler.unscale_, otherwise you clip scaled gradients against an unscaled threshold. And do not wrap the backward pass in autocast; only the forward and the loss.

Silent numerical failure

FP16 failures are rarely loud. Symptoms: the loss plateaus early while gradients are exactly zero in many layers (underflow); the loss suddenly becomes nan (overflow in activations or an unscaled gradient); validation accuracy is worse than FP32 by a few points (a precision-sensitive op ran in 16-bit). First step in debugging: run a few hundred steps in FP32 and compare loss curves. Second: use torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) for a short run to locate the first inf. Third: look at scaler.get_scale(); if it collapses toward 1 or keeps halving, gradients are overflowing every step.

Gradient accumulation

Memory limits the micro-batch size, but optimization often wants a larger batch (large-batch training stabilizes gradient estimates, and some recipes such as LLM pretraining prescribe hundreds of thousands of tokens per step). Gradient accumulation simulates a large batch by summing gradients over several micro-batches before one optimizer step.

The justification is the linearity of the gradient. For a loss that is a mean over B=A⋅bB=A\cdot bB=A⋅b examples, split into AAA micro-batches of size bbb:

∇θ1B∑i=1Bℓi  =  1A∑a=1A(1b∑i∈micro-batch a∇θℓi).\nabla_\theta \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\ell_i \;=\; \frac1A\sum_{a=1}^{A}\Bigl(\frac1b\sum_{i\in \text{micro-batch }a}\nabla_\theta\ell_i\Bigr).∇θ​B1​i=1∑B​ℓi​=A1​a=1∑A​(b1​i∈micro-batch a∑​∇θ​ℓi​).

PyTorch's backward() adds into .grad, so calling it AAA times and dividing each loss by AAA yields exactly the large-batch gradient (up to floating-point reordering). The weights are not changed in between, so the result is mathematically identical to one big batch for models whose forward pass is independent across examples.

pythonaccumulate.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Linear(20, 3)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
X, y = torch.randn(64, 20), torch.randint(0, 3, (64,))

# (a) one big batch of 64
opt.zero_grad()
F.cross_entropy(model(X), y).backward()
g_big = model.weight.grad.clone()

# (b) 4 micro-batches of 16, accumulated
opt.zero_grad()
A = 4
for xb, yb in zip(X.chunk(A), y.chunk(A)):
    (F.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb) / A).backward()      # divide so the sum is a mean
g_acc = model.weight.grad.clone()
print("max abs difference:", (g_big - g_acc).abs().max().item())   # about 1e-8

Three caveats. (1) Batch normalization computes statistics per micro-batch, so accumulation changes the model's behavior (use GroupNorm/LayerNorm, or accept the difference). (2) Per-example weighting: if the loss is a sum over tokens and micro-batches contain different numbers of non-padding tokens, dividing by AAA is wrong; normalize by the total token count of the full batch. (3) Distributed training: with DDP every backward() triggers an all-reduce, which is wasteful for the first A−1A-1A−1 micro-batches; wrap them in with model.no_sync(): and synchronize only on the last. The learning rate should be tuned for the effective batch size A⋅b⋅NGPUsA\cdot b\cdot N_{\text{GPUs}}A⋅b⋅NGPUs​; the linear scaling rule (Goyal et al., 2017) with a warm-up is the usual starting point (Week 3).

Gradient checkpointing

Where training memory goes

Backpropagation needs the intermediate activations of the forward pass, so they are kept until the backward pass reaches them. For a network of nnn layers with activations of size aaa each, activation memory is n⋅an\cdot an⋅a, which grows with batch size, sequence length and depth. Parameters, gradients and optimizer states do not depend on batch size; activations do, and for transformers with long sequences they dominate. Gradient checkpointing (also called activation recomputation or rematerialization; Chen, Xu, Zhang and Guestrin, 2016) stores only a subset of the activations and recomputes the others during the backward pass.

Deriving the square-root trade-off

Memory and compute of checkpointing a chain

Consider a chain of nnn layers, each with the same activation size (one unit) and the same forward cost ccc. Split it into kkk equal segments of n/kn/kn/k layers. In the forward pass we keep only the kkk segment inputs (the checkpoints) and discard everything else. During backward, we process segments from last to first. For each segment, we (1) re-run its forward pass from the checkpoint, storing its n/kn/kn/k internal activations, (2) backpropagate through it, (3) free those activations.

Memory. At peak we hold all kkk checkpoints plus the activations of one segment: M(k)  =  k+nk.M(k) \;=\; k + \frac{n}{k}.M(k)=k+kn​. Optimum. Differentiating, M′(k)=1−n/k2=0M'(k)=1-n/k^2=0M′(k)=1−n/k2=0 gives k⋆=nk^\star=\sqrt nk⋆=n​ and M(k⋆)=2nM(k^\star)=2\sqrt nM(k⋆)=2n​. For n=64n=64n=64 layers that is 16 units instead of 64. For n=1000n=1000n=1000, about 63 instead of 1000.

Compute. Every layer's forward pass is executed twice (once originally and once during recomputation), except layers in the last segment whose activations could be kept. The extra cost is at most one additional forward pass. Since a backward pass costs about twice a forward pass, one training step costs about cn(1+2)=3cnc n(1+2)=3cncn(1+2)=3cn without checkpointing and 4cn4cn4cn with it: roughly 33% more time for a memory reduction from O(n)O(n)O(n) to O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​).

Chen et al. also gave a recursive variant that reaches O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) memory at O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) extra compute. In practice the n\sqrt nn​ rule is used loosely: you checkpoint every transformer block (n checkpoints of one residual-stream tensor each) and recompute the block's internal activations (attention scores, MLP hidden states), which are by far the largest.

pythoncheckpoint_demo.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint, checkpoint_sequential

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.net(x)

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=1024, n=24, ckpt=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(d) for _ in range(n))
        self.ckpt = ckpt
    def forward(self, x):
        for blk in self.blocks:
            # use_reentrant=False is the recommended implementation (supports kwargs, nested autograd)
            x = checkpoint(blk, x, use_reentrant=False) if (self.ckpt and self.training) else blk(x)
        return x

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    x = torch.randn(32, 512, 1024, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
    for ckpt in (False, True):
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
        net = Net(ckpt=ckpt).cuda().train()
        net(x).sum().backward()
        print(f"checkpointing={ckpt}: peak {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**30:.2f} GiB")
        del net
# Alternative for nn.Sequential: checkpoint_sequential(seq, segments=int(len(seq) ** 0.5), input=x, use_reentrant=False)

On a transformer, selective recomputation (recompute only the cheap-but-large attention internals, store the expensive matmul outputs) recovers most of the memory saving for a smaller compute penalty (Korthikanti et al., 2022). Two cautions: dropout and other random operations must be replayed with the same random state during recomputation (PyTorch's checkpoint saves and restores RNG state by default), and layers with side effects such as batch-norm running statistics are updated twice.

What does a transformer activation actually cost?

For one transformer layer with sequence length sss, micro-batch bbb, hidden size hhh and aaa heads, and 16-bit activations, Korthikanti et al. (2022) count about s b h (34+5as/h)s\,b\,h\,(34 + 5as/h)sbh(34+5as/h) bytes. The second term is the s×ss\times ss×s attention matrices, which grow quadratically in sequence length. For h=4096h=4096h=4096, a=32a=32a=32, s=2048s=2048s=2048, b=4b=4b=4: 34+5⋅32⋅2048/4096=11434+5\cdot32\cdot2048/4096=11434+5⋅32⋅2048/4096=114, so about 2048⋅4⋅4096⋅114≈3.82048\cdot4\cdot4096\cdot114\approx3.82048⋅4⋅4096⋅114≈3.8 GB per layer, and 122 GB for 32 layers. That is why long-context training needs checkpointing and FlashAttention (which removes the quadratic term). Try it in the calculator below, where you can also see the model states.

InteractiveTraining memory calculator: parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations

Distributed training

When a model or the desired throughput exceeds one device, we spread the work. There are four basic axes of parallelism, and large runs combine them.

Strategy What is split What is replicated Communication Main use
Data parallel (DP/DDP) the batch the whole model all-reduce of gradients, once per step scale throughput when the model fits one GPU
Sharded data parallel (ZeRO, FSDP) the batch, plus optimizer states, gradients, parameters nothing (at stage 3) reduce-scatter and all-gather model too big to replicate, no model code changes
Tensor (intra-layer) parallel each weight matrix activations (partly) all-reduce inside every layer very large layers, needs fast NVLink
Pipeline parallel groups of layers (stages) nothing point-to-point activations between stages very deep models across nodes

Data parallelism and all-reduce

In data parallelism every one of NNN workers holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of the batch. Each computes a local gradient gr\boldsymbol g_rgr​; the workers then compute the average gˉ=1N∑rgr\bar{\boldsymbol g}=\frac1N\sum_r\boldsymbol g_rgˉ​=N1​∑r​gr​ (an all-reduce) and each applies the same optimizer update. Because all workers start from the same weights, use the same average gradient, and run deterministic optimizers, the replicas stay identical forever. The result equals single-device training on the combined batch, which makes data parallelism the safest way to scale.

Cost of ring all-reduce

Let the gradient have SSS bytes and let each GPU have a link of bandwidth β\betaβ to its ring neighbours. Split the gradient into NNN chunks of S/NS/NS/N bytes. Reduce-scatter: in each of N−1N-1N−1 steps every GPU sends one chunk to its right neighbour and adds the chunk received from the left into its own copy. After N−1N-1N−1 steps each GPU holds one chunk that is the complete sum over all GPUs. All-gather: in N−1N-1N−1 further steps the finished chunks circulate around the ring until every GPU has all of them. Each phase sends (N−1)⋅S/N(N-1)\cdot S/N(N−1)⋅S/N bytes per GPU, so

bytes sent per GPU=2(N−1)NS,tallreduce≈2(N−1)NSβ  →N→∞  2Sβ.\text{bytes sent per GPU}=\frac{2(N-1)}{N}S,\qquad t_{\text{allreduce}}\approx\frac{2(N-1)}{N}\frac{S}{\beta}\;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\;\frac{2S}{\beta}.bytes sent per GPU=N2(N−1)​S,tallreduce​≈N2(N−1)​βS​N→∞​β2S​.

The remarkable property is that the per-GPU traffic is nearly independent of NNN: adding GPUs does not make the all-reduce more expensive per GPU (ignoring latency terms and link contention). A naive scheme in which every worker sends its gradient to a parameter server would need O(N)O(N)O(N) traffic through one link. As an example, a 1.3B-parameter model has S=2.6S=2.6S=2.6 GB in BF16; at 300 GB/s effective NVLink the all-reduce takes about 2×2.6/300≈172\times2.6/300\approx 172×2.6/300≈17 ms, while across a 25 GB/s network it takes about 0.2 s, comparable with a whole step.

Ring all-reduce for deep learning was popularized by Baidu (2017); it builds on bandwidth-optimal collective algorithms (Patarasuk and Yuan, 2009). Tree-based and hierarchical variants reduce latency across many nodes. NCCL implements all of them.

DistributedDataParallel (DDP) in PyTorch

torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel implements data parallelism with one process per GPU. It groups parameters into buckets (default 25 MB) and launches the all-reduce of a bucket as soon as all its gradients are ready, overlapping communication with the backward pass. This is why DDP is far faster than the older single-process DataParallel, which should not be used.

pythonddp_train.py
# Launch with:  torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 ddp_train.py
import os, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSampler

def main():
    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")                 # torchrun sets RANK, WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR/PORT
    rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()
    local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)
    torch.manual_seed(0)                                    # identical init on every rank (DDP also broadcasts rank 0)

    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)).cuda(local_rank)
    model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank])
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)

    X = torch.randn(4096, 32); y = X.sum(1, keepdim=True)
    ds = TensorDataset(X, y)
    sampler = DistributedSampler(ds, num_replicas=world, rank=rank, shuffle=True)   # disjoint shard per rank
    loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=64, sampler=sampler, num_workers=2, pin_memory=True)

    accum = 2
    for epoch in range(3):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)                            # reshuffle differently each epoch (easy to forget)
        for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(loader):
            xb, yb = xb.cuda(local_rank, non_blocking=True), yb.cuda(local_rank, non_blocking=True)
            last = (i + 1) % accum == 0
            ctx = model.no_sync() if not last else torch.enable_grad()   # skip all-reduce on non-final micro-batches
            with ctx:
                loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(xb), yb) / accum
                loss.backward()
            if last:
                opt.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        if rank == 0:                                       # log / save only on one rank
            print(f"epoch {epoch} loss {loss.item() * accum:.4f}")
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The effective batch size is 64×N×accum64\times N\times\text{accum}64×N×accum. Common DDP mistakes are forgetting set_epoch, saving checkpoints from all ranks, using model.state_dict() keys with the module. prefix when reloading into an unwrapped model, and logging metrics from one rank as if they were global averages (use dist.all_reduce to average them).

Large-batch scaling

Data parallelism with NNN GPUs multiplies the global batch size. Beyond a "critical batch size" extra samples per step give diminishing returns in steps saved, so scaling the batch without limit wastes compute; Goyal et al. (2017) trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet with batch 8192 using linear LR scaling and warm-up, and LAMB/LARS-style optimizers extend this further. The theory is outside our scope, but the practical rule is to tune the learning rate and warm-up when NNN changes.

Tensor (model) parallelism

When a single layer is too big, or when you want to cut per-GPU activation memory, split the matrices. Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019) shows how to do this for a transformer MLP with a single all-reduce per block. The MLP computes Y=GeLU(XA)BY=\text{GeLU}(XA)BY=GeLU(XA)B with A∈Rd×4dA\in\R^{d\times 4d}A∈Rd×4d, B∈R4d×dB\in\R^{4d\times d}B∈R4d×d.

  • Split AAA by columns into [A1,A2][A_1, A_2][A1​,A2​] (one per GPU). Each GPU computes GeLU(XAi)\text{GeLU}(XA_i)GeLU(XAi​) for its slice of the hidden units independently. Because GeLU is elementwise, no communication is needed: the nonlinearity commutes with a column split (it would not commute with a row split, since GeLU of a sum is not the sum of GeLUs).
  • Split BBB by rows into B1,B2B_1,B_2B1​,B2​, matching the column slices. GPU iii computes Zi=GeLU(XAi)Bi∈Rb×dZ_i=\text{GeLU}(XA_i)B_i\in\R^{b\times d}Zi​=GeLU(XAi​)Bi​∈Rb×d, a partial sum of the output: Y=Z1+Z2Y=Z_1+Z_2Y=Z1​+Z2​.
  • One all-reduce sums the partial outputs.

Self-attention is split the same way: each GPU holds a subset of heads (the Q,K,VQ,K,VQ,K,V projections are column-split by head, the output projection row-split), again with one all-reduce at the end. A transformer layer therefore needs two all-reduces in the forward and two in the backward pass, each of size (batch × sequence × ddd). That traffic is on the critical path (it cannot overlap easily with compute), so tensor parallelism is only efficient within a node over NVLink, typically with degree 2 to 8.

Pipeline parallelism and the bubble

Pipeline parallelism places consecutive groups of layers on different devices (stages). Only activations (forward) and their gradients (backward) cross device boundaries, which is cheap enough to work across nodes. The problem is that stage 2 cannot start until stage 1 has finished, so with a single batch only one device works at a time. GPipe (Huang et al., 2019) splits each batch into mmm micro-batches and pipelines them: while stage 2 processes micro-batch 1, stage 1 already works on micro-batch 2. The first and last devices still idle at the start and end of each step; this idle time is the bubble.

Bubble fraction

Let each micro-batch take one time unit for the forward pass and (say) the same for backward through one stage, with ppp stages and mmm micro-batches. The ideal time (all devices always busy) is mmm units forward plus mmm backward. In GPipe the last stage cannot start the first micro-batch until p−1p-1p−1 units have elapsed, so the forward phase takes m+p−1m+p-1m+p−1 units; the backward phase likewise takes m+p−1m+p-1m+p−1. The idle fraction is

bubble=(m+p−1)−mm+p−1=p−1m+p−1.\text{bubble}=\frac{(m+p-1)-m}{m+p-1}=\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}.bubble=m+p−1(m+p−1)−m​=m+p−1p−1​.

For p=8p=8p=8 stages, m=8m=8m=8 micro-batches wastes 7/15=47%7/15=47\%7/15=47%; m=64m=64m=64 wastes 7/71=10%7/71=10\%7/71=10%. To make the bubble small you need m≫pm\gg pm≫p, but each micro-batch must also be large enough to keep a GPU busy, so the global batch size must be large. The bubble does not depend on how the model is split as long as stages are balanced.

A second cost is memory: GPipe must hold activations of all mmm micro-batches until their backward passes start. The 1F1B schedule (PipeDream-Flush; Narayanan et al., 2019 and 2021) alternates one forward and one backward pass in steady state, so a stage never holds more than ppp micro-batches of activations, while the bubble stays at (p−1)/(m+p−1)(p-1)/(m+p-1)(p−1)/(m+p−1). Interleaved schedules assign several small non-contiguous chunks of layers to each device, dividing the bubble by the number of chunks at the price of more communication. Try the simulator to see all of this.

InteractivePipeline schedules: bubble and stored activations

3D parallelism in practice

Training models with hundreds of billions of parameters (Megatron-Turing NLG, the BLOOM and Llama families) uses all three together: tensor parallelism within a node (fast NVLink), pipeline parallelism across nodes (cheap point-to-point traffic), and data parallelism across replicas of the whole pipeline, usually with sharded optimizer states. Narayanan et al. (2021) describe how to choose the degrees t,p,dt, p, dt,p,d with t⋅p⋅d=NGPUst\cdot p\cdot d=N_{\text{GPUs}}t⋅p⋅d=NGPUs​ and report about 52% of peak throughput on 3072 A100 GPUs for a one-trillion-parameter model. Sequence/context parallelism (splitting the sequence dimension) and expert parallelism (Mixture-of-Experts, below) are additional axes.

ZeRO and FSDP: sharding the redundancy

Memory accounting for mixed-precision Adam

In plain data parallelism every GPU stores the full model state, which is wasteful. Consider a model with Ψ\PsiΨ parameters trained with Adam and mixed precision. Per parameter you store:

  • FP16/BF16 parameters: 2 bytes
  • FP16/BF16 gradients: 2 bytes
  • Optimizer states in FP32: a master copy of the parameters (4 bytes), Adam's first moment mmm (4) and second moment vvv (4): 12 bytes, called K=12K=12K=12 in the ZeRO paper.

Total 16Ψ16\Psi16Ψ bytes, before activations. For Ψ=7.5\Psi=7.5Ψ=7.5 B that is 120 GB. The optimizer states alone are 75% of it. This is a lot of memory that is identical on every GPU.

ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer; Rajbhandari, Rasley, Ruwase and He, SC 2020) removes the redundancy by partitioning model states over the NNN data-parallel ranks, in three cumulative stages:

  • Stage 1 (PosP_{os}Pos​): shard the optimizer states. Each rank owns 1/N1/N1/N of them and updates the corresponding 1/N1/N1/N of the parameters, then an all-gather distributes the updated parameters. Memory: 4Ψ+12Ψ/N4\Psi+12\Psi/N4Ψ+12Ψ/N.
  • Stage 2 (Pos+gP_{os+g}Pos+g​): also shard the gradients. Gradients are reduce-scattered so that each rank receives only the (averaged) shard it owns. Memory: 2Ψ+14Ψ/N2\Psi+14\Psi/N2Ψ+14Ψ/N.
  • Stage 3 (Pos+g+pP_{os+g+p}Pos+g+p​): also shard the parameters. Each rank stores only 1/N1/N1/N of the parameters. Before a layer runs, its full parameters are all-gathered; after use they are freed. Memory: 16Ψ/N16\Psi/N16Ψ/N.

Communication cost

Baseline DDP all-reduces gradients: 2Ψ2\Psi2Ψ elements per step in ring terms (reduce-scatter Ψ\PsiΨ + all-gather Ψ\PsiΨ). ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 use a reduce-scatter of gradients (Ψ\PsiΨ) and an all-gather of updated parameters (Ψ\PsiΨ): the same 2Ψ2\Psi2Ψ as DDP, so memory savings are free in volume. ZeRO-3 additionally all-gathers parameters in the forward pass (Ψ\PsiΨ) and again in the backward pass (Ψ\PsiΨ, since they were freed), plus the gradient reduce-scatter (Ψ\PsiΨ): 3Ψ3\Psi3Ψ, a 1.5x increase over DDP. In exchange the model-state memory shrinks linearly with NNN. The overhead is hidden by prefetching the next layer's parameters while the current layer computes.

FSDP in PyTorch

FullyShardedDataParallel (FSDP) is PyTorch's implementation of the ZeRO-3 idea (Zhao et al., "PyTorch FSDP", VLDB 2023). Its sharding unit is a wrapped module; you choose the wrapping granularity with an auto-wrap policy, typically one transformer block per unit so that only one block's full parameters are materialized at a time.

pythonfsdp_train.py
# torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 fsdp_train.py
import os, functools, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP, MixedPrecision, ShardingStrategy
from torch.distributed.fsdp.wrap import ModuleWrapPolicy

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln(x))

def main():
    dist.init_process_group("nccl")
    local = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]); torch.cuda.set_device(local)
    model = nn.Sequential(*[Block(2048) for _ in range(24)])          # about 1.2B parameters

    bf16 = MixedPrecision(param_dtype=torch.bfloat16,                 # compute/all-gather in BF16
                          reduce_dtype=torch.bfloat16,                # gradient reduce-scatter in BF16
                          buffer_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    model = FSDP(model,
                 auto_wrap_policy=ModuleWrapPolicy({Block}),          # one FSDP unit per Block
                 sharding_strategy=ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD,       # ZeRO-3 (SHARD_GRAD_OP is ZeRO-2)
                 mixed_precision=bf16,
                 device_id=torch.cuda.current_device())
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)              # create AFTER wrapping: optimizer states are sharded
    x = torch.randn(8, 512, 2048, device="cuda")
    for step in range(5):
        loss = model(x).float().pow(2).mean()
        loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        if dist.get_rank() == 0:
            print(step, loss.item(), f"peak mem {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**30:.1f} GiB")
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Newer PyTorch releases add a per-parameter-sharding API, torch.distributed.fsdp.fully_shard ("FSDP2"), with the same ideas; DeepSpeed implements ZeRO with additional offloading of states to CPU memory or NVMe (ZeRO-Offload, ZeRO-Infinity). Rule of thumb for choosing: if the model plus optimizer fit on one GPU, use DDP (fastest). If they do not, use FSDP/ZeRO-3 across the data-parallel group. Add tensor and pipeline parallelism only when you cross many nodes or when even one layer is too large.

Run the calculator again with ZeRO stages and a fixed 8-GPU budget to find which stage first fits a 7B model on 40 GB or 80 GB cards.

Efficient attention: FlashAttention

Why standard attention is slow

Recall single-head attention for a sequence of length NNN with head dimension ddd (Week 9): S=QK⊤/d∈RN×NS=QK^\top/\sqrt d\in\R^{N\times N}S=QK⊤/d​∈RN×N, P=softmax⁡(S)P=\softmax(S)P=softmax(S) row-wise, O=PVO=PVO=PV. The textbook implementation runs three kernels. It computes SSS and writes it to HBM (N2N^2N2 numbers), reads it back to compute softmax and writes PPP (N2N^2N2 more), and reads PPP again for the product with VVV. At N=8192N=8192N=8192, one head's score matrix has 67 million entries, 134 MB in FP16, for a computation whose inputs Q,K,VQ,K,VQ,K,V are only 3Nd=3×8192×64≈1.63Nd=3\times8192\times64\approx1.63Nd=3×8192×64≈1.6M numbers. The matmuls have high intensity, but softmax and the surrounding data movement are memory-bound and the N2N^2N2 intermediate dominates both time and memory.

The key observation of FlashAttention (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra and Ré, NeurIPS 2022) is that attention is IO-bound, not FLOP-bound, and that the exact same result can be computed tile by tile in SRAM without ever materializing SSS or PPP in HBM. The obstacle is softmax, which needs the whole row to normalize. The solution is the online softmax.

Online softmax

Online (streaming) softmax

For a row of scores s1,…,sNs_1,\dots,s_Ns1​,…,sN​ the numerically stable softmax is pj=esj−m/ℓp_j=e^{s_j-m}/\ellpj​=esj​−m/ℓ with m=max⁡jsjm=\max_j s_jm=maxj​sj​ and ℓ=∑jesj−m\ell=\sum_j e^{s_j-m}ℓ=∑j​esj​−m. Naively this needs one pass for mmm, one for ℓ\ellℓ, one to normalize. Milakov and Gimelshein (2018) observed that mmm and ℓ\ellℓ can be maintained in a single streaming pass. Suppose after seeing the first ttt scores we have mt=max⁡j≤tsjm_t=\max_{j\le t}s_jmt​=maxj≤t​sj​ and ℓt=∑j≤tesj−mt\ell_t=\sum_{j\le t}e^{s_j-m_t}ℓt​=∑j≤t​esj​−mt​. A new score st+1s_{t+1}st+1​ arrives. Set mt+1=max⁡(mt,st+1)m_{t+1}=\max(m_t,s_{t+1})mt+1​=max(mt​,st+1​). The old sum was computed relative to mtm_tmt​, so rescale it to the new reference:

ℓt+1=ℓt emt−mt+1+est+1−mt+1.\ell_{t+1}=\ell_t\,e^{m_t-m_{t+1}}+e^{s_{t+1}-m_{t+1}}.ℓt+1​=ℓt​emt​−mt+1​+est+1​−mt+1​.

Check: ℓtemt−mt+1=∑j≤tesj−mtemt−mt+1=∑j≤tesj−mt+1\ell_t e^{m_t-m_{t+1}}=\sum_{j\le t}e^{s_j-m_t}e^{m_t-m_{t+1}}=\sum_{j\le t}e^{s_j-m_{t+1}}ℓt​emt​−mt+1​=∑j≤t​esj​−mt​emt​−mt+1​=∑j≤t​esj​−mt+1​, so ℓt+1=∑j≤t+1esj−mt+1\ell_{t+1}=\sum_{j\le t+1}e^{s_j-m_{t+1}}ℓt+1​=∑j≤t+1​esj​−mt+1​. The same rescaling works when scores arrive in blocks.

Including the value-weighted sum. What attention actually needs is o=∑jpjvjo=\sum_j p_j v_jo=∑j​pj​vj​. Define the unnormalized accumulator o~t=∑j≤tesj−mtvj\tilde o_t=\sum_{j\le t}e^{s_j-m_t}v_jo~t​=∑j≤t​esj​−mt​vj​. Exactly as for ℓ\ellℓ, o~t+1=o~t emt−mt+1+est+1−mt+1vt+1,\tilde o_{t+1}=\tilde o_t\,e^{m_t-m_{t+1}}+e^{s_{t+1}-m_{t+1}}v_{t+1},o~t+1​=o~t​emt​−mt+1​+est+1​−mt+1​vt+1​, and at the end o=o~N/ℓNo=\tilde o_N/\ell_No=o~N​/ℓN​. So a single pass over keys and values, carrying only the running triple (m,ℓ,o~)(m,\ell,\tilde o)(m,ℓ,o~) per query row, gives the exact attention output.

The tiled algorithm

FlashAttention applies this recursion to blocks. Partition QQQ into row blocks QiQ_iQi​ (of BrB_rBr​ rows) and K,VK,VK,V into blocks Kj,VjK_j,V_jKj​,Vj​ (of BcB_cBc​ rows), with block sizes chosen so that a QiQ_iQi​, a KjK_jKj​, a VjV_jVj​ and the Br×BcB_r\times B_cBr​×Bc​ score tile all fit in SRAM. Then, for each query block iii (outer loop) and each key/value block jjj (inner loop):

  1. Load Qi,Kj,VjQ_i,K_j,V_jQi​,Kj​,Vj​ from HBM into SRAM.
  2. Compute the tile Sij=QiKj⊤/dS_{ij}=Q_iK_j^\top/\sqrt dSij​=Qi​Kj⊤​/d​ in SRAM.
  3. Update the running row maxima minew=max⁡(mi,rowmax(Sij))m_i^{\text{new}}=\max(m_i,\text{rowmax}(S_{ij}))minew​=max(mi​,rowmax(Sij​)).
  4. Compute P~ij=exp⁡(Sij−minew)\tilde P_{ij}=\exp(S_{ij}-m_i^{\text{new}})P~ij​=exp(Sij​−minew​) and ℓi←emi−minewℓi+rowsum(P~ij)\ell_i\leftarrow e^{m_i-m_i^{\text{new}}}\ell_i+\text{rowsum}(\tilde P_{ij})ℓi​←emi​−minew​ℓi​+rowsum(P~ij​).
  5. Update the accumulator O~i←emi−minewO~i+P~ijVj\tilde O_i\leftarrow e^{m_i-m_i^{\text{new}}}\tilde O_i+\tilde P_{ij}V_jO~i​←emi​−minew​O~i​+P~ij​Vj​.

After the last jjj, write Oi=O~i/ℓiO_i=\tilde O_i/\ell_iOi​=O~i​/ℓi​ and the row logsumexp Li=mi+log⁡ℓiL_i=m_i+\log\ell_iLi​=mi​+logℓi​ to HBM. The N×NN\times NN×N matrices never leave SRAM.

pythonflash_attention_numpy.py
import numpy as np

def attention_reference(Q, K, V):
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[1])
    S = S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    P = np.exp(S); P /= P.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return P @ V

def flash_attention(Q, K, V, Br=16, Bc=32):
    """Exact attention computed tile by tile with the online-softmax recursion (forward pass only)."""
    N, d = Q.shape
    O = np.zeros_like(Q)
    L = np.zeros(N)                                    # row logsumexp, saved for the backward pass
    for i in range(0, N, Br):                          # outer loop over query blocks
        Qi = Q[i:i + Br]
        m = np.full(Qi.shape[0], -np.inf)              # running row max
        l = np.zeros(Qi.shape[0])                      # running row sum of exp
        acc = np.zeros_like(Qi)                        # running unnormalized output
        for j in range(0, N, Bc):                      # inner loop over key/value blocks
            Sij = Qi @ K[j:j + Bc].T / np.sqrt(d)      # (Br, Bc) tile: lives in "SRAM"
            m_new = np.maximum(m, Sij.max(axis=1))
            P = np.exp(Sij - m_new[:, None])
            scale = np.exp(m - m_new)                  # rescale old statistics to the new max
            l = scale * l + P.sum(axis=1)
            acc = scale[:, None] * acc + P @ V[j:j + Bc]
            m = m_new
        O[i:i + Br] = acc / l[:, None]
        L[i:i + Br] = m + np.log(l)
    return O, L

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, d = 200, 64                                         # N not divisible by the block sizes on purpose
Q, K, V = (rng.standard_normal((N, d)) for _ in range(3))
O_ref = attention_reference(Q, K, V)
O_fl, L = flash_attention(Q, K, V)
print("max abs error vs reference:", np.abs(O_ref - O_fl).max())     # about 1e-15

The result is exact, not an approximation. The causal mask is handled by skipping tiles that are entirely above the diagonal (which saves about half the work) and masking within diagonal tiles.

Why it is faster, and what it costs

Let MMM be the SRAM size. Standard attention does Θ(Nd+N2)\Theta(Nd+N^2)Θ(Nd+N2) HBM accesses. FlashAttention does Θ(N2d2/M)\Theta(N^2d^2/M)Θ(N2d2/M) accesses: each of the N/BrN/B_rN/Br​ outer iterations streams all of K,VK,VK,V once, and the block size scales as Br∼M/dB_r\sim M/dBr​∼M/d, so the total is NBr⋅Nd=N2d2M\frac{N}{B_r}\cdot Nd=\frac{N^2d^2}{M}Br​N​⋅Nd=MN2d2​. Since d2≪Md^2\ll Md2≪M for typical values (d=64d=64d=64 to 128128128, M≈100M\approx 100M≈100 KB), this is a large reduction. The FLOP count is unchanged (slightly higher, from the rescaling) but the kernel becomes compute-bound instead of memory-bound. The memory footprint drops from O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) to O(N)O(N)O(N), enabling much longer contexts. Dao et al. reported 2 to 4 times wall-clock speed-ups on attention and 15% end-to-end speed-up on BERT-large training at that time.

For the backward pass, FlashAttention does not store PPP. It stores only OOO and LLL and recomputes SSS and PPP tile by tile from Q,K,VQ,K,VQ,K,V and LLL (Pij=exp⁡(Sij−Li)P_{ij}=\exp(S_{ij}-L_i)Pij​=exp(Sij​−Li​)). This is the same compute-for-memory trade as checkpointing, but it is a net speed-up because recomputation in SRAM is cheaper than reading N2N^2N2 numbers from HBM. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) improved work partitioning across thread blocks and warps, and FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024) exploits Hopper-specific asynchrony and FP8. You rarely write this yourself: torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention dispatches to a fused FlashAttention kernel when the inputs allow it (CUDA, FP16/BF16, supported head sizes).

pythonsdpa.py
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

B, H, N, d = 2, 8, 4096, 64
q, k, v = (torch.randn(B, H, N, d, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(3))

# Fused, memory-efficient attention: never builds the (N x N) matrix.
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)

def naive(q, k, v):
    s = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / d ** 0.5
    mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(N, N, device=q.device, dtype=torch.bool), 1)
    return (s.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf")).softmax(-1)) @ v

print("max diff:", (out.float() - naive(q, k, v).float()).abs().max().item())
for name, fn in [("fused", lambda: F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)), ("naive", lambda: naive(q, k, v))]:
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(); fn(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(name, f"peak {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**20:.0f} MiB")

KV caching and speculative decoding

Autoregressive decoding and the KV cache

A decoder-only language model generates one token at a time. Computing the attention output for token ttt requires the keys and values of all tokens 1..t1..t1..t. Recomputing them at every step would cost O(t)O(t)O(t) projections per token, O(T2)O(T^2)O(T2) overall. Since keys and values of earlier tokens never change (causal masking), we cache them. At each step we compute only the query, key and value of the newest token, append kt,vtk_t,v_tkt​,vt​ to the cache, and attend over the cache. Per-token compute becomes O(t)O(t)O(t) for the attention itself and O(1)O(1)O(1) for everything else.

The cache costs memory. For one token, each layer stores a key and a value for each KV head:

KV bytes per token=2⋅nlayers⋅nkv heads⋅dhead⋅b.\text{KV bytes per token}=2\cdot n_{\text{layers}}\cdot n_{\text{kv heads}}\cdot d_{\text{head}}\cdot b.KV bytes per token=2⋅nlayers​⋅nkv heads​⋅dhead​⋅b.

For a Llama-2-7B-like configuration (32 layers, 32 heads of dimension 128, FP16, b=2b=2b=2) that is 2⋅32⋅32⋅128⋅2=524,2882\cdot32\cdot32\cdot128\cdot2=524{,}2882⋅32⋅32⋅128⋅2=524,288 bytes, 0.5 MB per token. A 4096-token context costs 2 GiB per sequence, and 32 concurrent requests cost 64 GiB, more than the 13 GB of FP16 weights. At long context and large batch the KV cache, not the weights, is the memory bottleneck, and reading it every step makes decoding memory-bound.

The main remedies reduce the number of cached values or manage them better. Multi-query attention (Shazeer, 2019) shares one key/value head across all query heads; grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) shares a KV head among a group of query heads, a middle ground adopted by many open models. PagedAttention (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023; the basis of the vLLM server) stores the cache in fixed-size blocks like virtual-memory pages, removing the fragmentation that comes from reserving a maximum-length buffer per request. Cache quantization (int8/int4 keys and values) and sliding-window attention reduce it further.

pythonkv_cache.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class CachedSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=256, h=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.dk = h, d // h
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d); self.out = nn.Linear(d, d)

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        B, T, D = x.shape                                           # T = number of NEW tokens (1 when decoding)
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).view(B, T, 3, self.h, self.dk).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)   # each (B, h, T, dk)
        if cache is not None:
            k = torch.cat([cache[0], k], dim=2)                     # (B, h, T_past + T, dk)
            v = torch.cat([cache[1], v], dim=2)
        # With a cache, new queries may attend to all past keys, so no causal mask is needed when T == 1.
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=(cache is None and T > 1))
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, D)
        return self.out(y), (k, v)

torch.manual_seed(0)
attn = CachedSelfAttention().eval()
x = torch.randn(1, 10, 256)
with torch.no_grad():
    full, _ = attn(x)                                               # process all 10 tokens at once
    cache, outs = None, []
    for t in range(10):                                             # token by token with the cache
        o, cache = attn(x[:, t:t + 1], cache); outs.append(o)
    inc = torch.cat(outs, dim=1)
print("cached == full:", torch.allclose(full, inc, atol=1e-5), "| cache shape:", tuple(cache[0].shape))

Speculative decoding

Decoding is memory-bound: producing one token reads all the weights (13 GB for a 7B model in FP16) and uses almost none of the GPU's arithmetic (I≈1I\approx1I≈1 FLOP/byte, see above). Verifying γ\gammaγ tokens at once costs nearly the same time as generating one, because the weights are read once either way. Speculative decoding (Leviathan, Kalman and Matias, 2022; Chen et al., 2023) exploits this. A small, fast draft model proposes γ\gammaγ tokens autoregressively; the large target model scores all γ\gammaγ proposals in a single forward pass; a rejection-sampling rule accepts a prefix of the proposals and, at the first rejection, resamples from a corrected distribution. The rule guarantees that the output distribution is exactly the target model's, so quality is unchanged.

If each proposed token is accepted independently with probability α\alphaα (a simplification), the expected number of tokens produced per target forward pass is

E[tokens]=1−αγ+11−α,\mathbb E[\text{tokens}]=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha},E[tokens]=1−α1−αγ+1​,

since the verification pass always yields at least one token (the correction or a bonus token) and each further token requires all earlier ones to be accepted. With α=0.8,γ=4\alpha=0.8,\gamma=4α=0.8,γ=4 this is (1−0.85)/0.2=3.36(1-0.8^5)/0.2=3.36(1−0.85)/0.2=3.36 tokens per target pass, a speed-up of up to about 3x if the draft cost is small. The speed-up is greatest when the draft agrees often with the target (similar training data, an easy domain such as code or boilerplate) and when decoding is memory-bound. Variants avoid a separate draft model by adding extra prediction heads to the target (Medusa), or by drafting with early layers of the same network. At large batch sizes the GPU is already compute-bound, and speculation helps less.

Model compression

Compression reduces the cost of a trained model: fewer parameters, fewer bits per parameter, or a cheaper architecture with similar behavior. The four classical families are pruning, quantization, distillation and low-rank factorization. They are largely orthogonal and often stacked (Han, Mao and Dally's Deep Compression, ICLR 2016, combined pruning, quantization and Huffman coding to shrink AlexNet 35x and VGG-16 49x without accuracy loss on ImageNet). A key practical lesson, which applies to everything below, is that a reduction in parameter count or theoretical FLOPs is not a reduction in latency unless the hardware and kernels can exploit it.

Pruning

Pruning removes weights (or larger structures) that contribute little. The earliest work (LeCun, Denker and Solla's Optimal Brain Damage, 1989) estimated the loss increase from deleting each weight with a second-order Taylor expansion. The simplest modern criterion is magnitude pruning: remove the weights with the smallest ∣w∣|w|∣w∣, on the assumption that small weights matter least. Han et al. (2015) showed that the loop train, prune, fine-tune, repeat ("iterative pruning") can remove 80 to 90% of the weights of many convolutional networks with little loss.

  • Unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights anywhere. It reaches the highest sparsity for a given accuracy, but the result is an irregular sparse matrix, and dense GPU kernels gain nothing from it: a matrix with 90% zeros takes the same time as a dense one unless special sparse kernels are used (which usually pay off only above ~90% sparsity). NVIDIA's Ampere GPUs support a hardware-accelerated 2:4 structured sparsity pattern (exactly two non-zeros in every four consecutive weights), which can give up to about 2x matmul speed-up at 50% sparsity.
  • Structured pruning removes whole units: convolution filters, attention heads, neurons or even entire layers. The remaining network is a smaller dense network and runs faster on any hardware. It costs more accuracy per removed parameter, and you must re-wire the dimensions of adjacent layers. Importance scores include the filter's ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ or ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ norm, the BatchNorm scale γ\gammaγ ("network slimming"; Liu et al., 2017) or a first-order saliency ∣w ∂L/∂w∣|w\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial w|∣w∂L/∂w∣.
  • Global versus layerwise pruning. Comparing magnitudes across layers (global threshold) lets the algorithm decide how much each layer can lose; per-layer fixed ratios are simpler but wasteful. The first and last layers are usually more sensitive and are often left dense.
pythonprune_demo.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.utils.prune as prune

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 10))

# Unstructured: zero the 70% smallest-|w| weights in each Linear, using a global threshold.
params = [(m, "weight") for m in model if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
prune.global_unstructured(params, pruning_method=prune.L1Unstructured, amount=0.7)

# Structured: remove 25% of the output neurons (rows) of the first layer, ranked by L2 norm.
prune.ln_structured(model[0], name="weight", amount=0.25, n=2, dim=0)

for i in (0, 2):
    w = model[i].weight                         # now = weight_orig * weight_mask (a reparametrization)
    print(f"layer {i}: sparsity {(w == 0).float().mean().item():.2%}")

# During fine-tuning the mask stays fixed. When done, make pruning permanent:
for m, name in params:
    prune.remove(m, name)                       # folds the mask into .weight, deletes weight_orig/weight_mask
print("params remain dense tensors:", model[0].weight.shape)   # zeros are still stored!

Note the last line: PyTorch's pruning utilities mask weights; they do not make the tensor smaller or faster. To get real savings with structured pruning you must physically slice the weight matrices (or use a toolkit such as torch-pruning), and for unstructured pruning you must convert to a sparse format or 2:4 layout.

The lottery ticket hypothesis

Frankle and Carbin (ICLR 2019) found that dense networks contain small sub-networks ("winning tickets") which, when reset to their original initialization (or, for larger models, to an early-training checkpoint) and trained in isolation, can match the dense network's accuracy. This suggested that overparameterization helps optimization and that much of the final network is redundant. It remains an empirical observation about trained-from-scratch sparse networks, with subtleties at scale, but it motivated much research on pruning at initialization.

Quantization

Quantization stores weights (and possibly activations) as low-bit integers instead of 16- or 32-bit floats. It shrinks memory 2 to 8 times, reduces the bandwidth cost of every memory-bound operation (recall the decode roofline), and, when the hardware has integer tensor-core instructions, speeds up the arithmetic too.

Uniform affine quantization and its error

Given a real range [α,β][\alpha,\beta][α,β] to be represented with bbb bits (2b2^b2b levels), the affine (asymmetric) scheme uses a scale sss and an integer zero-point zzz: s=β−α2b−1,z=round⁡ ⁣(−αs),wq=clip⁡(round⁡(w/s)+z,  0,  2b−1),w^=s (wq−z).s=\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2^b-1},\quad z=\operatorname{round}\!\Bigl(-\frac{\alpha}{s}\Bigr),\quad w_q=\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\operatorname{round}(w/s)+z,\;0,\;2^b-1\bigr),\quad \hat w=s\,(w_q-z).s=2b−1β−α​,z=round(−sα​),wq​=clip(round(w/s)+z,0,2b−1),w^=s(wq​−z). The symmetric scheme fixes z=0z=0z=0 and uses a range [−α,α][-\alpha,\alpha][−α,α] with α=max⁡∣w∣\alpha=\max|w|α=max∣w∣: s=α/(2b−1−1)s=\alpha/(2^{b-1}-1)s=α/(2b−1−1), wq=clip⁡(round⁡(w/s),−(2b−1−1),2b−1−1)w_q=\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(w/s),-(2^{b-1}-1),2^{b-1}-1)wq​=clip(round(w/s),−(2b−1−1),2b−1−1). For int8 this gives levels −127..127-127..127−127..127, for int4, −7..7-7..7−7..7.

Error. Rounding to the nearest level gives an error e=w−w^e=w-\hat we=w−w^ in [−s/2,s/2][-s/2,s/2][−s/2,s/2]. If the weights are spread widely over many levels, eee is approximately uniform and E[e2]=s2/12\mathbb E[e^2]=s^2/12E[e2]=s2/12. Taking a range 2α2\alpha2α split into 2b2^b2b levels, s=2α/2bs=2\alpha/2^bs=2α/2b and the noise power is α23 2−2b\frac{\alpha^2}{3}\,2^{-2b}3α2​2−2b. If the signal has power σw2\sigma_w^2σw2​, SQNR=σw2α22−2b/3  ⇒  SQNR (dB)=10log⁡103σw2α2+6.02 b.\text{SQNR}=\frac{\sigma_w^2}{\alpha^2 2^{-2b}/3}\;\Rightarrow\;\text{SQNR (dB)}=10\log_{10}\frac{3\sigma_w^2}{\alpha^2}+6.02\,b.SQNR=α22−2b/3σw2​​⇒SQNR (dB)=10log10​α23σw2​​+6.02b. Each extra bit buys about 6 dB (a factor 4 in noise power, 2 in RMS error). The first term shows the price of range: if an outlier makes α≫σw\alpha\gg\sigma_wα≫σw​, you lose precision for every weight that shares that scale.

Granularity therefore matters a great deal. Per-tensor quantization uses one scale for the whole matrix; per-channel (per output row) uses one per row; group-wise uses one per group of 32 to 128 consecutive weights within a row (the standard for 4-bit LLM weights), at a cost of 16 bits of scale per group (0.125 to 0.5 extra bits per weight). Run the explorer below with an outlier and compare:

InteractiveQuantization explorer: bits, granularity, outliers
pythonquant_numpy.py
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# 512 output channels whose scales differ (log-normal), plus one outlier weight: typical of real layers.
W = rng.standard_normal((512, 512)) * np.exp(0.7 * rng.standard_normal((512, 1)))
W[3, 7] = 12.0

def quantize_sym(W, bits, axis=None):
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
    scale = np.abs(W).max(axis=axis, keepdims=True) / qmax        # per-tensor if axis=None, per-row if axis=1
    Wq = np.clip(np.round(W / scale), -qmax, qmax)                # the stored integers
    return Wq.astype(np.int8), scale

def rel_rmse(W, Wq, scale):
    return np.sqrt(((W - Wq * scale) ** 2).mean() / (W ** 2).mean())

print("bits  per-tensor  per-channel")
for bits in (8, 6, 5, 4, 3):
    r_t = rel_rmse(W, *quantize_sym(W, bits, axis=None))
    r_c = rel_rmse(W, *quantize_sym(W, bits, axis=1))
    print(f"{bits:4d}  {r_t:10.4f}  {r_c:11.4f}")

Post-training quantization (PTQ)

PTQ quantizes an already-trained model without retraining. Weights are easy: pick scales from their ranges. Activations are harder because their ranges depend on the input. Dynamic quantization computes the activation scale at run time from each tensor's actual min/max (no calibration, a little overhead). Static quantization runs a few hundred calibration batches through the model to record activation ranges (min/max, a percentile, or a range minimizing KL divergence or MSE to the float values) and fixes the scales. Integer matmuls then accumulate in int32 and are rescaled: with y=∑kxkwky=\sum_k x_k w_ky=∑k​xk​wk​ and x≈sxxqx\approx s_x x_qx≈sx​xq​, w≈swwqw\approx s_w w_qw≈sw​wq​ we get y≈sxsw∑kxq,kwq,ky\approx s_xs_w\sum_k x_{q,k}w_{q,k}y≈sx​sw​∑k​xq,k​wq,k​, an integer dot product times one floating-point factor (Jacob et al., CVPR 2018, the scheme behind TensorFlow Lite and PyTorch's fbgemm/qnnpack backends).

pythonptq_dynamic.py
import io, torch, torch.nn as nn

def size_mb(m):
    buf = io.BytesIO(); torch.save(m.state_dict(), buf); return buf.getbuffer().nbytes / 2**20

torch.manual_seed(0)
fp32 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 1024), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(1024, 1024), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(1024, 10)).eval()

# Dynamic PTQ: int8 weights (per-tensor by default), activations quantized on the fly. CPU inference.
int8 = torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic(fp32, {nn.Linear}, dtype=torch.qint8)

x = torch.randn(64, 784)
with torch.no_grad():
    d = (fp32(x) - int8(x)).abs().max().item()
print(f"size: {size_mb(fp32):.2f} MB -> {size_mb(int8):.2f} MB   max|logit diff| = {d:.4f}")
print(int8[0])      # DynamicQuantizedLinear(in_features=784, out_features=1024, dtype=torch.qint8, ...)

Quantization-aware training (QAT)

PTQ breaks down at very low bit widths or for sensitive architectures. QAT simulates quantization during training so that the network learns weights that are robust to it. The forward pass applies fake quantization, w^=s clip⁡(round⁡(w/s))\hat w=s\,\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(w/s))w^=sclip(round(w/s)), while the weights themselves remain floats. The difficulty is that round⁡\operatorname{round}round has zero gradient almost everywhere. The straight-through estimator (STE) (Bengio, Léonard and Courville, 2013) pretends round⁡\operatorname{round}round is the identity in the backward pass, so that ∂w^/∂w≈1\partial\hat w/\partial w\approx 1∂w^/∂w≈1 inside the clipping range and 000 outside. After training, the real integers are exported.

pythonqat_ste.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class FakeQuant(torch.autograd.Function):
    """Symmetric per-tensor fake quantization with a straight-through gradient."""
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, w, bits):
        qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
        scale = w.detach().abs().max().clamp_min(1e-8) / qmax
        ctx.save_for_backward(w.detach().abs() <= qmax * scale)       # inside the clip range?
        return torch.clamp(torch.round(w / scale), -qmax, qmax) * scale
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, g):
        (inside,) = ctx.saved_tensors
        return g * inside, None                                       # STE: pass gradient through where not clipped

class QLinear(nn.Linear):
    def __init__(self, i, o, bits=4):
        super().__init__(i, o); self.bits = bits
    def forward(self, x):
        return F.linear(x, FakeQuant.apply(self.weight, self.bits), self.bias)

torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.randn(2048, 20); y = (X[:, :5].sum(1) > 0).long()           # toy classification
for bits in (None, 4, 2):
    lin = (lambda i, o: QLinear(i, o, bits)) if bits else nn.Linear
    net = nn.Sequential(lin(20, 64), nn.ReLU(), lin(64, 2))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 1e-2)
    for _ in range(300):
        loss = F.cross_entropy(net(X), y); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    print(f"bits={bits}: train acc {(net(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item():.3f}")

PyTorch's torch.ao.quantization offers eager-mode and FX-graph workflows (prepare_qat, convert) that insert observers and fake-quant modules and fuse patterns such as Conv-BN-ReLU; the lab below uses the simplest route. QAT is a short fine-tune (a few epochs at a small learning rate) starting from a trained float model.

8-bit and 4-bit quantization of large language models

LLMs revealed a new problem: their activations contain a few outlier features, hidden dimensions whose magnitudes are 10 to 100 times larger than the rest, which wreck per-tensor activation quantization. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., NeurIPS 2022) handles this by decomposing the matmul: the few outlier columns are computed in FP16, the rest in int8 with per-row/per-column scales.

At 4 bits and below, weights are quantized while activations stay in 16 bits (weight-only quantization), which is exactly what the memory-bound decode regime needs: bytes read per token drop 4x. Two influential post-training methods:

  • GPTQ (Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler and Alistarh, 2022; ICLR 2023) quantizes a layer's weights one column at a time and, after rounding each, adjusts the not-yet-quantized weights to compensate for the error it caused, using second-order information (the Hessian of the layer's squared output error, H=2XX⊤H=2XX^\topH=2XX⊤, estimated from a few hundred calibration samples). It descends from the Optimal Brain Surgeon line of work and quantizes 175B-parameter models to 3 or 4 bits in a few GPU-hours.
  • AWQ (Lin et al., 2023; MLSys 2024), activation-aware weight quantization, observes that a small fraction (about 1%) of weight channels matter disproportionately because they multiply large activations. Rather than keeping them in high precision, it scales those channels up before quantization (and the corresponding activations down), reducing their relative rounding error. The scale is chosen by a small search on calibration data.

QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) combines a 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) base model, whose 16 levels are placed at quantiles of a normal distribution because pretrained weights are roughly Gaussian, with LoRA adapters (Week 10), making it possible to fine-tune a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU.

Evaluate quantized models on what matters

Average perplexity or top-1 accuracy can hide damage on long-tail behaviors: rare classes, reasoning chains, long contexts, multilingual text. Evaluate the compressed model on the task metrics you care about and on a few hard slices, and always compare latency on the target hardware, since a 4-bit model on a GPU without a fast dequantization kernel can be slower than FP16.

Knowledge distillation

Distillation (Bucilua, Caruana and Niculescu-Mizil, 2006; Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015) trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. Why is this better than training the student on the labels alone? Because the teacher's output distribution carries more information than a one-hot label: for an image of a BMW, the teacher might give 0.9 to "BMW", 0.09 to "other car" and 10−610^{-6}10−6 to "carrot". Those relative small probabilities ("dark knowledge") describe the similarity structure of the classes. But with a confident teacher the small probabilities are so tiny that they barely affect the loss. Hinton et al. fix this with a temperature TTT: divide the logits ziz_izi​ by TTT before the softmax,
